source.title: Scaling Open Discrete Audio Foundation Models with Interleaved Semantic, Acoustic, and Text Tokens
source.authors: Potsawee Manakul; Woody Haosheng Gan; Martijn Bartelds; Guangzhi Sun; William B. Held; Di-Yi Yang

record.tranche_reason: The study applies an IsoFLOP sweep and held-out validation-loss analysis to discrete audio models, testing compute allocation and loss scaling with a different modality and model set.
record.gate_note: The paper reports relevant results from its 64-model IsoFLOP sweep, loss fits, and larger SODA runs. Other ablations and cited scaling results are not included unless they bear on a claim version.
record.test_reason: The study runs a Chinchilla-style IsoFLOP sweep (64 models, 3e18–3e20 FLOPs) and a parametric loss fit on discrete audio token LMs. It derives compute-optimal allocation exponents, checks extrapolation to 4 larger runs, and correlates held-out NLL with downstream metrics. The method matches the originals, but the setting is a new modality, so this is T3 rather than T1.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right but incomplete. The authors conclude that optimal data scales about 1.6× faster than model size, which they attribute to the lower information density of audio tokens. They say NLL reliably predicts downstream performance even at larger scales, while absolute loss extrapolations from the IsoFLOP regime are imperfect. They also find that capabilities scale differently: cross-modal and acoustic skills saturate, while semantic and text knowledge show accelerating gains. Separately, cold-start training beats warm-start for audio tasks.
record.recipe_differences: Uses an IsoFLOP sweep and held-out loss analysis analogous to compute-scaling studies, but tests decoder-only discrete audio models with interleaved semantic, acoustic, and text tokens rather than text-only LLMs.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted exponents differ somewhat between IsoFLOP fitting and the alternative parametric loss fit; predictions from the smaller compute range diverge for larger final runs.
record.problems: The IsoFLOP study covers 3 × 10^18 to 3 × 10^20 FLOPs, and the authors note that its smaller-scale regime may affect the fitted exponent. Larger-run loss extrapolations are inaccurate. The paper reports one run per configuration for the warm-start comparison, but that limitation is not central to the scaling sweep.
record.rows_left_out: No additional scaling-related result rows left out. Design-choice, warm-start, and fine-tuning results do not measure the claim versions recorded here.

untested.parts: Text-only language model loss scaling; this study is on discrete audio token models only.
Extrapolation for text LMs; extrapolation here spans only about 1.5 orders of magnitude of compute.
Text-model allocation; Kaplan vs Hoffmann exponents are not re-measured on text.
All of it; depth and width are not varied at fixed N.
Image and video, repeated-data laws, and fine-tuning or transfer scaling. The S2ST fine-tuning is not a scaling study.
Parameter counting, learning-rate schedule, and dataset variations as sources of exponent differences.

missing.what: Whether the 4 final SODA runs fall on the NLL→downstream regression lines fitted on the 64 IsoFLOP models. They largely follow the lines, but ASR and Salmon fall off one side (diminishing returns) and HellaSwag and sWUGGY the other (emergence).
missing.locator: Section 5.1 'Extrapolation to Larger Scale'; Figure 3; Section 6.2.2

missing.what: The compute-optimal tokens-per-parameter ratio rises from about 13 at 1e20 FLOPs to about 58 at 1e23 (projected), compared with Chinchilla's roughly constant 20.

record.verdict_notes: R5–R8 compare over-trained models with the compute-optimal frontier, so they cannot test V2. R9 is the real extrapolation test, and its state is partial, not reversed. Audio-token rows are linked to V5 rather than V1, because V1 names text language-model pretraining. R4's positive exponent is likely a sign lost in text extraction.

versions.untested_parts: Text-only language models and separate scaling in parameters, tokens, or compute outside the discrete-audio setting.
Extrapolation for text-only language models; the larger runs are SODA audio models.
The study does not test the Kaplan or Hoffmann text-model allocation exponents directly.
Image and video models, fine-tuning and transfer, and other non-audio training regimes.
Downstream-task predictability outside the tested audio and text benchmarks.
The effects of alternative parameter-counting conventions, training schedules, or datasets beyond the setup variations reported.

rows.note: The authors report that optimal data scales faster than optimal model size.

rows.subject: 64 discrete audio IsoFLOP models
